title: Bugs
summary: Introduces the origin of the term 'bug' in computing, showing the famous first computer bug found in a relay of the Harvard Mark II.
main_text: Bugs. The original 'bug'. The slide shows a photograph of a logbook page from September 9, 1947, documenting the first actual case of a bug being found. A moth was found trapped in Relay #70, Panel F of the Harvard Mark II computer. The handwritten log entry reads: 'First actual case of bug being found.' This incident is widely cited as the origin of the term 'bug' in computing, though the term was used informally before this event.
notes_text: Grace Hopper's team is often credited with this discovery. The logbook page with the moth taped to it is preserved at the Smithsonian.

images.description: Photograph of a historical logbook page from September 9, 1947, showing handwritten entries and a moth taped to the page. The entry documents the first actual case of a computer bug being found in Relay #70, Panel F of the Harvard Mark II.
labels: First actual case of bug being found

title: Step 1: Review your Own Code
summary: Introduces rubber duck debugging as the first debugging strategy: explain your code line by line to yourself or an inanimate object to find errors.
main_text: Step 1: Review your Own Code. Rubber Duck Debugging: Reference from an anecdote from a book, 'The Pragmatic Programmer', that has become popular. Idea: Explain your code line by line to yourself or some other 'object'. Note: Commenting your code is a way to do this. The concept is that by forcing yourself to articulate what each line of code does, you will naturally discover logical errors and misunderstandings in your own code. Walking through your code can help you find the bug.
notes_text: Rubber duck debugging is a well-known technique from 'The Pragmatic Programmer' by Andrew Hunt and David Thomas. The idea is that explaining code out loud forces you to think more carefully about each step.

images.description: Meme image of a rubber duck with text reading 'Explain your code to an inanimate object' and 'Walking through your code can help you find the bug', illustrating the rubber duck debugging concept.
labels: EXPLAIN YOUR CODE TO AN INANIMATE OBJECT
WALKING THROUGH YOUR CODE CAN HELP YOU FIND THE BUG

title: Step 2: Test Cases and Expected Outputs
summary: Explains the importance of creating test cases that cover different code paths and determining expected output before debugging.
main_text: Step 2: Test Cases & Expected Outputs. Determine input test case(s) that will exercise various parts of your code. Each if/else block. When the loop executes 0, 1, or more times. Determine the expected output. You cannot effectively debug without an expectation of the right output so you know when the program is working. Before you can identify what is wrong, you need to know what the correct behavior should be. Test cases should cover edge cases and different branches of your program.
notes_text: This step is critical because many students try to debug without knowing what the correct output should be, making it impossible to verify fixes.

title: Step 3: Tracing
summary: Demonstrates hand-tracing code execution using a variable table to walk through code line by line with a failing input scenario.
main_text: Step 3: Tracing. Use one of your input scenarios that is not working and trace the execution of your code by hand. Make a table of variables and walk the code line by line. The slide shows a C++ program that checks if a number is prime. The code includes: #include <iostream>, #include <cmath>, using namespace std; int main() { int n; cout << "Enter an integer:" endl; cin >> n; bool isPrime; isPrime = true; for(int i=2; i < sqrt(n); i++) { if(n % i == 0) { isPrime = false; break; } } if(isPrime) { cout << "Prime" << endl; } else { cout << "Not prime" << endl; } return 0; }. A variable tracking table with columns for i, n, and isPr(ime) is shown alongside the code for recording values during manual tracing.
notes_text: Note the bug in this code: the loop condition uses i < sqrt(n) instead of i <= sqrt(n), which would fail for perfect squares like 9 (since sqrt(9)=3 and the loop stops before checking i=3).

images.description: A code listing showing a C++ prime-checking program in a yellow/tan code box, alongside an empty variable tracking table with columns labeled i, n, and isPr. The table is meant for students to fill in values as they trace through the code manually.

title: Step 4: Print Statements / Narration
summary: Explains using print statements to narrate program execution, placing them in control structures to verify flow and variable values.
main_text: Step 4: Print Statements / Narration. Let the computer 'trace' for you by using print statements. Now that you know what to expect, the most common and easy way to find the error is to add print statements that will 'narrate' where you are and what the variable values are. Be a detective by narrowing down where the error is. Put a print statement in each 'for', 'while', 'if' or 'else' block...this will make sure you are getting to the expected areas of your code. Then print variable values so you can see what data your program is producing.
notes_text: Print statement debugging (also called printf debugging) is one of the most widely used debugging techniques at all skill levels. The key insight is to use print statements strategically in control flow blocks to verify both the path of execution and the data being processed.

images.description: Cartoon illustration of a detective character with a magnifying glass, representing the idea of being a detective when debugging code by narrowing down where errors occur.

title: Tips
summary: Provides practical advice for writing and debugging programs incrementally: write small portions, compile, test, then add more.
main_text: Tips. Don't write the entire program all at once. Write a small portion, compile and test it. Write the code to get the input values, add some couts to print out what you got from the user, and make sure it is what you expect. Write a single loop and test it before doing nested loops. Once one part works, add another part and test it. The key principle is incremental development: build and verify your program in small, testable pieces rather than writing everything and then trying to debug a large, complex program all at once.
notes_text: Incremental development is especially important for beginners who may struggle to debug large programs. Testing input handling first is a practical starting point.

title: Codio Debugger
summary: Section divider slide introducing the Codio Debugger tool, transitioning from general debugging strategies to using a specific debugger tool.
main_text: Codio Debugger. This section introduces the Codio debugger, a built-in debugging tool available in the Codio online IDE used in the course.
notes_text: Codio is the online development environment used in CS102. The following slides cover how to use its built-in debugger.

title: Debuggers
summary: Describes the core capabilities of debugger tools: setting breakpoints, stepping through code line by line, and viewing variable values.
main_text: Debuggers. Allows you to: Set a breakpoint (the code will run and then stop when it reaches the certain line of code). Step through your code line by line so that you can see where the flow of the program goes. Show variable values when you have stopped at a certain line of code. Debuggers automate the manual tracing process by letting the computer pause execution at specified points, allowing you to inspect the program state at each step.
notes_text: This slide summarizes the three fundamental features common to all debuggers, not just Codio's. These same capabilities exist in VS Code, GDB, LLDB, and other debugging tools.

title: Starting the Debugger
summary: Explains how to launch the Codio debugger using the 'Debug Current File' button and what happens when the program encounters an error.
main_text: Starting the Debugger. In Codio, use the 'Debug Current File' on the far right of the top menu bar to launch the debugger targeting the file your cursor is in. When you run the program, it highlights the exact line where the code breaks. Thus, whenever the code does not run as you expect or want, one of your first steps should be: Run the debugger.
notes_text: The 'Debug Current File' button is specific to Codio's interface. The debugger will compile with debug symbols automatically.

images.description: Screenshot of the Codio 'Debug Current File' button, shown as a dark blue button with a bug icon and dropdown arrow on the right side of the menu bar.

title: Breakpoints
summary: Explains how to set breakpoints in Codio by clicking the code margin, causing execution to pause at specified lines for variable inspection.
main_text: Breakpoints. Allows you to specify lines of code where you want the flow to stop and analyse the values of the variables/function calls/etc. In Codio, you can set it up by clicking on the margin of the code and see a red dot appear at the line of the code. The slide shows a code example with line numbers 35-41, where line 36 shows 'int main() {' highlighted in red/pink, and line 37 has a red breakpoint dot set on 'int vals[10] = {9, 7, 14, 20, 2, 8,...'. Other visible lines include: line 38 'cout << "Enter a number: ";', line 39 'int num;', line 40 'cin >> num;'.
notes_text: Breakpoints are non-destructive and do not modify your source code, unlike print statements. You can add and remove them freely during a debugging session.

images.description: Screenshot of Codio code editor showing a C++ program with line numbers 35-41. Line 36 (int main) is highlighted in pink/red. Line 37 has a red breakpoint dot in the margin next to an array initialization. The code includes variable declarations and cin/cout statements.

title: Debugger Commands
summary: Describes the four main debugger commands: Run, Step Over (Next), Step Out, and Step Into, along with the debugger panel showing call stack, variables, watches, and breakpoints.
main_text: Commands. Run: Runs the program (until breakpoint). Note: it will pause temporarily when at a cin statement and wait for you to type the input. Step Over (Next): Run the current line and pause at the next line of code. Step Out: Finishes (step out of) the current function's code (or hit the breakpoint), and then pause at the next line of the previous function on the stack. Step Into: If current line is a function, it steps into the function pausing at the first line of the function body. If current line is not a function, it executes the line (like step over). The debugger panel on the right side shows: Program is paused status, Call Stack showing reverse.cpp(36)main(), Local variables displaying vals, num, and loc values, Watches section with no watch expressions, Breakpoints section, and Console.
notes_text: Step Over is the most commonly used command for basic debugging. Step Into is essential when you suspect a bug is inside a function call. Step Out is useful when you have stepped into a function and want to return to the caller quickly.

images.description: Screenshot of the Codio debugger panel on the right side of the IDE showing the program paused state. The panel displays sections for Call Stack (showing reverse.cpp(36)main()), Local variables (showing vals array values, num: 1431653565, loc: 21845), Watches (no watch expressions), Breakpoints, and Console. Debugger control buttons (Run, Step Over, Step Into, Step Out, Stop) are visible at the top.

title: Showing Values
summary: Demonstrates how the debugger displays local variable values that update in real-time as you step through program execution.
main_text: Showing Values. We can view the value of local variables which will update as we step through the program. The Local variables panel shows the current values: vals: (-136422928, 32767, 0, 0, 1431653488, 21845, 143...), num: 1431653565, loc: 21845. These values represent uninitialized variable states before the program has assigned meaningful values to them. As you step through code, these values will change to reflect the actual computations being performed.
notes_text: The garbage values shown (like 1431653565 for num) are typical of uninitialized variables in C++. This is a good demonstration of why variables should always be initialized before use.

images.description: Screenshot of the Codio debugger Local variables panel showing three variables: vals (an array with values including -136422928, 32767, 0, 0, 1431653488, 21845, 143...), num (1431653565), and loc (21845). These are uninitialized values displayed before program execution assigns them.

title: Function Call Stack (Not Covered)
summary: Introduces the call stack view in the debugger, showing how function calls are tracked and how local variables can be inspected per function frame.
main_text: Function Call Stack (Not Covered). Allows you to see the functions being called and what the system stack looks like. For example here, the 'main()' function calls 'reverseAndFind()'. We can view the value of local variables in each function by clicking that function in the stack area. The Call Stack panel shows: reverse.cpp(15)reverseAndFind() at the top of the stack, and reverse.cpp(42)main() below it. The Local variables panel shows: vals: (-136422928, 32767, 0, 0, 1431653488, 21845, 143...), num: 1431653565, loc: 21845. By clicking different functions in the call stack, you can switch context and see the local variables belonging to that particular function's scope.
notes_text: This topic is marked 'Not Covered' indicating it may be revisited in a later unit or is provided as supplementary material. The call stack is fundamental to understanding how functions execute and return in C++.

images.description: Two screenshots from the Codio debugger. The top screenshot shows the Call Stack panel with two entries: reverse.cpp(15)reverseAndFind() and reverse.cpp(42)main(), indicating main called reverseAndFind. The bottom screenshot shows the Local variables panel with vals, num, and loc values for the selected stack frame.
